question: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}$ be defined by $f(x) = \frac{x-2}{x-3}$. Prove whether $f$ is one-one and/or onto.
explanation:
To check injectivity, assume $f(a)=f(b)$.

$\frac{a-2}{a-3}=\frac{b-2}{b-3}$.

Cross multiplying gives $(a-2)(b-3)=(b-2)(a-3)$.

Expanding and simplifying leads to $a=b$.

Thus $f$ is one-one.

To check surjectivity, let $y=\frac{x-2}{x-3}$.

Then $y(x-3)=x-2$.

Thus $yx-3y=x-2 \Rightarrow x(y-1)=3y-2$.

Hence $x=\frac{3y-2}{y-1}$ which is defined for $y \ne 1$.

Since every $y \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{1\}$ has a corresponding $x$, the function is onto.

Therefore $f$ is bijective.

options.C: $f$ is both one-one and onto, so it is bijective
